A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CURIO research. Text extraction and visual inspection support comparison of the complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices A–F in v2 and A–G in v3.

before.justification: v2 reports original training and evaluation results for Exercise Recommendation and Education Dialogue, including Tables 1–3, learning curves, and appendix analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds human evaluation results for Education Dialogue in Appendix B.1 and Table 6.

M1.justification: CURIO's user modeling, intrinsic reward variants, model components, and multi-turn optimization remain unchanged. Moving the optimization description from Section 3.2.2 to Appendix A.1 does not change the procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use Exercise Recommendation and Education Dialogue with the same represented user traits and learning styles. Human judges assess existing kinds of simulated educational conversations; this changes evaluation procedures, not dialogue task or population coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding automated comparisons retain the same SFT, MTRLHF, and reward-variant membership. The added human study evaluates the already compared MTRLHF, DiffAcc, and DiffLogAcc methods, introducing no new comparator.

E3.justification: v3 introduces a substantial human evaluation protocol: 10 students assess 60 conversations spanning 20 topic/user settings, with shuffled model presentation and separate personalization and quality ratings. Appendix B.1 describes pairwise comparisons, whereas Appendix G specifies 1–5 ratings without explaining their conversion. Existing training and automated evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds a limited validation analysis comparing human preferences with Auto Eval. Existing reward-variant analyses, user-type breakdowns, question distributions, and conversational case studies are retained. The new imperfect-user-model interpretation does not introduce a robustness experiment.

E5.justification: v3 introduces formal uncertainty reporting absent from v2: exact two-sided binomial tests and 95% confidence intervals for human DiffLogAcc–MTRLHF comparisons. Appendix B.1 reports personalization preference 0.76, CI [0.69, 0.82], p < .001, and quality preference 0.45, CI [0.38, 0.52], p = .179. No additional training-run or seed reporting appears.

E6.justification: New Table 6 adds two human-preference matrices, substantially extending the outcome evidence beyond automated evaluation. DiffLogAcc's human win rates against MTRLHF are 75.75% for personalization and 45.00% for quality. The corresponding automated rates, 75.95% and 54.43%, and other original results remain unchanged; these are different-evaluator results, not same-setting performance changes.

T1.justification: The POMDP formulation, PBRS theorem, potential functions, and Appendix C combinatorial-bandit argument are retained. Optimization equations are relocated and condensed, and potential functions share one numbered display, without substantive mathematical revision.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements, and concluding research claims retain the same meaning: curiosity-driven user modeling improves personalization and generalization while maintaining conversation quality. Human evaluation supplies new support rather than redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: v3 interprets human preferences as supporting Auto Eval's validity and the nonsignificant quality result as showing no quality reduction. It also interprets the existing Figure 4 as evidence that CURIO works with imperfect user models. Static-trait and simulated-user limitations remain, while the planned future comprehensive human evaluation is removed.

D1.justification: New Appendix G documents the human-study instructions, survey template, shuffled presentation, 1–5 scales, 30–60-minute duration, $15 compensation, and reported IRB approval. Existing model choices, hyperparameters, data-generation code, and prompts are retained; moving optimization details adds no new training disclosure.

R1.justification: Both versions cite the same 33 works and retain their substantive positioning relative to personalized RLHF and intrinsic motivation. Reference reordering and a shortened related-work passage do not change the claimed relationship to prior research.

P1.justification: v3 moves the optimization subsection into Appendix A, inserts human-study sections, and makes localized prose, heading, acknowledgment, and conference-header edits. The overall narrative and most existing text remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds human-results Table 6 and a survey template, relocates existing displays, and compresses equation presentation. All five original figure assets are unchanged, and existing result tables retain their substantive structure despite relocation and renumbering.

improvement.justification: Human judgments and survey documentation add useful support for personalization beyond v2's automated evaluation. The gain is limited by unexplained rating-to-win conversion and Table 6's 75.75% preference rate conflicting with Appendix B.1's 152/200. Furthermore, the 45% quality preference and confidence interval establish no detected difference, rather than proving preserved quality. These weaknesses temper the benefit of the added evidence.
